tldr: The authors introduce OmniCAD, the first large-scale benchmark of 25k mechanical CAD assemblies across industrial systems such as robotics and automotive components to evaluate vision-language models (VLMs) on assembly reasoning. Comprehensive testing of leading frontier models reveals that they struggle severely with handling repeated parts, millimeter-level precision, and recovering geometric mate constraints.
hero_caption: Failure cases where leading VLMs are given a part library and a completed visual target to assemble components. Parts interpenetrate and collide, poses and orientations drift, and required parts are missing—highlighting the fragility of spatial and geometric reasoning compared to human engineering ground truth.
overview:
In recent years, vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in object recognition and everyday task planning. However, whether they can accurately reason about the assembly of complex physical mechanisms, such as robotic hardware and industrial machinery, has remained largely underexplored. Prior assembly research has focused primarily on furniture manuals, which feature small part counts and are too simplistic to capture tight geometric constraints and strict manufacturing tolerances.

To address this gap, the authors established OmniCAD, the first large-scale benchmark spanning diverse industrial machinery across robotics, automotive, aerospace, and agricultural equipment. Sourced from 25,000 real-world SolidWorks mechanical CAD assemblies, it systematically organizes an average of 12 part instances, 21 mate relationship types, and multi-view rendered images.

Using this benchmark, the authors comprehensively evaluated nine frontier VLMs, including Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview. In addition to a one-shot setup that predicts assembly poses directly, they implemented an agentic evaluation framework where models iteratively self-correct using re-rendered images and geometric collision-checking tools.

Experimental results show that while current models can capture coarse rotations to some extent, they struggle immensely with reusing identical parts multiple times, achieving millimeter-level positioning, and identifying geometric mate constraints between components. Even with interactive tool-based refinements, adjustments remain coarse, and over half of the assemblies still suffer from part interpenetration, underscoring significant hurdles ahead for practical robotic assembly reasoning.
contributions: Constructed OmniCAD, the first large-scale 3D mechanical assembly reasoning benchmark, featuring 25,000 real-world CAD assemblies and 289,000 mate constraints across robotic mechanisms and industrial machinery.
Formulated a comprehensive assembly reasoning evaluation across part identification, 6-DoF pose estimation, mate graph recovery, and external tool-augmented self-correction.

Benchmarked nine open-weight and proprietary frontier VLMs under a unified pipeline, demonstrating clear limitations in repeated part utilization, millimeter-level translation, and collision prevention.

sections.heading: Moving from flatpack furniture to serious industrial robotic mechanisms
sections.summary: Existing 3D assembly benchmarks have been biased toward furniture datasets with few parts and simple connections, falling short of industrial mechanical systems. This paper introduces OmniCAD, a 25k-assembly benchmark spanning robotics and aerospace, to test the true spatial reasoning capabilities of VLMs.
sections.details:
While multimodal AI continues to advance in image generation and digital content understanding, assembly reasoning—correctly putting physical parts together to create a functional structure—remains largely uncharted territory. Most prior work has focused on household furniture like IKEA sets, which come with illustrative manuals, small part counts, and straightforward connectivity.

Real-world industrial machinery, such as robotic arms, automotive drivetrains, and aerospace hardware, presents fundamentally different challenges. Assemblies involve numerous visually similar components, dense geometric mates (concentric, coincident, parallel, etc.), extremely tight engineering tolerances, and complex insertion paths.

Prior CAD datasets primarily consisted of isolated part shapes lacking assembly constraint graphs, while vision-centric datasets lacked CAD boundary representations (B-Reps) and ground-truth geometric constraints.

To bridge this divide, the authors designed OmniCAD to examine whether modern VLMs can identify the exact parts needed from a library and correctly reconstruct their 6-DoF poses (position and orientation) along with part-to-part mating relationships, relying solely on completed target renderings and a part library.

captions.F2: OmniCAD benchmark statistics: (a) word cloud of application domains including robotics, manufacturing, and aerospace; (b) number of library part types per assembly (mean: 7.85); (c) total part instances per assembly (mean: 12.00); and (d) number of mate constraints per assembly (mean: 11.56).

sections.heading: From simple part placement to constraint-driven engineering assembly
sections.summary: Machine learning for 3D assembly has progressed from single-category placement to pairwise joint prediction. Yet, no existing benchmark covered part library identification, repeated instance reuse, millimeter-accurate 6-DoF placement, mate graph reasoning, and iterative tool use all at once.
sections.details:
Learning-based 3D part assembly began with part retrieval and placement, later evolving into relational graph pose prediction, generative models, and assembly sequence planning. In mechanical CAD, joint-aware methods such as AutoMate and JoinABLe emerged, but these primarily specialized in isolated part pairs or narrow categories.

A look at 3D dataset history shows an evolution from object-centric shapes like ShapeNet to standalone CAD repositories like ABC and DeepCAD. While assembly-oriented datasets such as PartNet-Assembly and Breaking Bad followed, none offered an end-to-end framework integrating native CAD geometric constraints, part library matching, and practical iterative refinement.

OmniCAD stands as the first benchmark designed to holistically evaluate part retrieval from libraries with repeated instances, strict 6-DoF placement from multi-view images, mate graph recovery, and tool-augmented self-correction loops.

sections.heading: Automating large-scale benchmark construction directly from real CAD files
sections.summary: Using SolidWorks assemblies collected from open CAD repositories, OmniCAD automatically extracts part hierarchies, geometric constraints, and multi-view renderings. The benchmark comprises four core evaluation tasks: part identification, 3D pose estimation, mate graph reasoning, and agentic refinement.
sections.details:
OmniCAD is built from real-world, engineer-verified CAD projects collected from open repositories including GrabCAD and 3D ContentCentral. All data originate in native SolidWorks assembly (.SLDASM) and part (.SLDPRT) formats, widely used across manufacturing industries.

The authors built a scalable automated annotation pipeline using the SolidWorks API to extract the following information systematically:
- Part metadata: deduplicated library part IDs, per-instance IDs, meshes, and ground-truth 3D positions and orientations in the assembly coordinate frame.
- Assembly constraints: 21 mate constraint edge types, including concentric, coincident, parallel, perpendicular, distance, and angle, along with dependency graphs.
- Multimodal references: 8-view renderings taken from the vertices of a bounding view cube, part-segmented color-coded views, completed assembly OBJ meshes, and B-Rep (.STEP) data.

The resulting benchmark contains 25,000 assemblies, 300,000 part instances, 196,000 unique parts, and 289,000 mate constraints, establishing an unprecedented scale.

captions.F3: An overview of OmniCAD representation: from left to right, the deduplicated part library and mate relationship graph (Mate Graph), the ground-truth completed 3D model, and multi-view rendered images captured from the vertices of an enclosing view cube.

sections.heading: Scoring assemblies strictly: from millimeter alignment to physical collisions
sections.summary: To evaluate model predictions, the benchmark introduces multifaceted metrics including multiset part identification accuracy, millimeter-level translation and rotation errors, point cloud shape similarity, mate graph F1 scores, and a collision-free rate (C-Free) to penalize part interpenetration.
sections.details:
Evaluation goes beyond simple text matching, measuring true 3D geometric fidelity and engineering validity.

- Part Identification: In addition to multiset library matching (PartID), the benchmark tracks full recovery without repeated parts (ID-NR) and full recovery with repeated parts (ID-R) separately.
- Pose Estimation: Optimal matching is performed among instances sharing the same library ID to calculate the mean translation error (PosErr in mm). Fine precision is assessed using strict thresholds: translation error under 10 mm (Pos@10mm) and rotation error under 10 degrees (Rot@$10^{\circ}$).
- Shape Similarity: Evaluates surface-symmetric Chamfer Distance (CD) between sampled part point clouds, part accuracy within 10 mm (PA), and assembly-wide scene Chamfer Distance (SCD).
- Mate Graph Recovery: Measures multiset mate edge F1 score (PairF1), mate type classification accuracy (TypeAcc), and directed graph similarity (GSim).
- Physical Validity: Runs axis-aligned bounding box (AABB), oriented bounding box (OBB), and mesh intersection tests to compute the collision-free prediction rate (C-Free). API parse success rate (PR) and runtime (RT) are also recorded.

sections.heading: State of frontier models: rough orientations work, millimeter translations and collisions collapse
sections.summary: Testing nine frontier models including GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8 showed part identification accuracy plummeting from 95.1% to 26.4% when parts were repeated. Positional accuracy (Pos@10) peaked at only 27.9% in one-shot settings, and even with collision-checking tools, over half the assemblies still showed interpenetration.
sections.details:
The experiments benchmarked nine models across proprietary systems (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro, etc.) and open-weight models (Llama 4 Maverick, Qwen3.5-9B, etc.).

Key findings include:
- The Repeated-Part Wall: When parts appeared only once, part identification on color-coded views (ColorView) reached an average ID-NR of 95.1%. However, when parts were reused—such as identical screws or washers (ID-R)—accuracy crashed to an average of 26.4%. Models struggle significantly with instantiating identical parts multiple times.
- Translation vs. Rotation Disparity: Models captured coarse rotations (Rot@$10^{\circ}$) relatively well, but translation accuracy (Pos@10mm) peaked at only 27.9% in the one-shot setup (and 34.6% in the agentic setup). Millimeter-level spatial placement remains beyond current VLMs.
- Mate Graph Recovery: Predicting mating edges (PairF1 up to 46.1%) and reconstructing overall graph structure (GSim up to 23.3%) proved difficult. Supplying ground-truth mate graphs improved pose metrics, but was still insufficient on its own to resolve relative positioning.
- Limits of Agentic Refinement: Providing visual re-rendering tools (2DVis) and collision detection feedback (Conflict+2DVis) helped models rectify large pose errors, raising collision-free rates (C-Free) up to 43.8%. Nevertheless, more than half of the assemblies retained interpenetrating parts, showing that current tools fall short of fine tuning.
- Reliability and Cost: While Gemini 3.1 Pro achieved the highest PA (55.0%) with MG+Color, its schema-compliant API success rate was just 0.3%. Furthermore, agentic inference took over 280 seconds per assembly, posing significant practical cost challenges.

captions.F4: The agentic assembly reasoning framework used for evaluation: starting from initial inputs, the model outputs an assembly JSON, receives intermediate re-rendered views (2DVis) and collision reports (Conflict+2DVis) from external tools, and iteratively refines poses and mate constraints for up to 10 rounds.

sections.heading: Toward AI that can assemble the physical world
sections.summary: By establishing OmniCAD with 25k industrial CAD assemblies, this study uncovers critical gaps in the spatial and geometric reasoning of frontier VLMs. The benchmark provides an open evaluation foundation toward physically sound, robust assembly AI.
sections.details:
This work introduced OmniCAD, the first large-scale benchmark featuring 25,000 real-world mechanical assemblies complete with part libraries, engineer-verified ground-truth CAD models, multi-view images, and explicit mate constraint graphs.

Comprehensive one-shot and tool-assisted agent evaluations reveal that even top-tier VLMs face severe limitations in essential engineering capabilities: repeated part selection, millimeter-accurate spatial placement, physical collision avoidance, and mate constraint graph recovery.

The authors will open-source the benchmark dataset, evaluation code, and tool interfaces. This infrastructure aims to accelerate next-generation AI systems capable of not merely describing images, but designing, assembling, and repairing functional machines in the physical world.

takeaways: Even frontier VLMs with strong visual perception see dramatic accuracy drops when required to instantiate the same library part multiple times.
Millimeter-level translation is far harder for VLMs than predicting coarse rotations; visual cues alone fail to resolve precise spatial coordinates.
Iterative visual re-rendering and collision checking help correct coarse pose errors, but remain insufficient for meeting strict geometric engineering tolerances.

Automating robotic assembly and mechanical design will require tighter integration between language models and exact geometric constraint solvers or CAD kernels, rather than relying purely on heuristic reasoning.
limitations: Certain advanced models, such as Gemini 3.1 Pro, showed extremely low schema-compliant API success rates (PR), revealing a substantial gap between geometric capability and generation reliability.
The current agentic setup requires over 200 seconds per assembly, making the inference overhead too steep for direct real-time robotic manipulation.

Self-correction tools are restricted to bounding-box and mesh interference checks, lacking deeper integration with optimization solvers that can strictly resolve underlying CAD algebraic mate equations.
